## Paper

## Abstract

Modern agricultural robotic systems are constrained by limited sensing and manipulation capabilities, particularly in fruit harvesting, where variability in color, size, and firmness poses significant challenges. Existing solutions, often reliant on rigid grippers and single-modality sensors, frequently cause fruit bruising and substantial post-harvest losses. Here, we present a compact, five-finger soft robotic gripper with integrated multimodal sensing—including vision, tactile, and curvature sensing—for adaptive and non-destructive fruit harvesting. The system incorporates 13 sensors, onboard electronics, local computation, and a rotational harvesting module. Each finger embeds custom stretchable optical fibers functioning as tactile and curvature sensors, while the palm houses a miniaturized camera and distance sensor. The gripper actuates within two seconds at 80 kPa, exerts up to 6 N of pulling force, and lifts objects up to 1 kg—more than 16 times its own weight. Its workspace expands from 200 mm² to 14,000 mm², enabling the handling of fruits with diverse shapes and sizes. Each finger bends up to 240°, with performance closely matching finite element predictions. For vision measurements, the hue channel in the HSV color space enables robust real-time color detection, achieving 100% shape classification accuracy and a size measurement error below 1.8%. Tactile sensors distinguish soft from firm objects, while curvature sensors accurately measure the finger’s bending state—both based on optical signal loss. Real-time demonstrations validate the system’s ability to assess ripeness using multimodal data (vision, tactile, and curvature) and successfully harvest greenhouse strawberries with minimal damage. This platform offers a versatile, sensor-rich solution for both precision agriculture and general-purpose robotic manipulation.

---

## Introduction

Many fruits ripen at varying rates and are primarily inspected visually, relying on changes in skin color to determine optimal picking times for farm-to-market distribution. Some crops have acceptable quality for commercial harvest over a period of weeks (e.g., citrus), whereas others must be harvested within a day or two of achieving acceptable quality (e.g., strawberries, raspberries). Fruit harvested too early will not have good flavor and sweetness, whereas fruit harvested after the peak of ripeness may be too soft and spoil quickly. 1-4. Fruits that develop over a long period (e.g., pomegranate, citrus) are typically firmer, often have thicker skin, and are easier to inspect visually due to their slower spoilage rates. In contrast, fruits with shorter ripening periods (e.g., berries) are usually soft, often have thinner skin, and are more challenging to inspect visually because of their rapid transition from acceptable quality to spoilage. These differences contribute to substantial variation in postharvest losses in the supply chain, with approximately 6–7% loss for pomegranates and up to 25% for strawberries 4-7.

Visual assessment of fruit quality is not always feasible, as many fruits exhibit minimal or inconsistent changes in skin color that may not be associated with ripeness. For example, avocados and pawpaws do not reliably change from a green skin color during ripening and vary in ripening time. Avocados can be of an acceptable quality for harvest over a period of weeks, whereas pawpaws become too soft in days after they ripen, leading to high spoilage rates during distribution. Postharvest losses of avocados can reach up to 24% 8, and pawpaws, despite being delicious, are only distributed locally because of their short storage life and ease of bruising.

Tactile inspections are an alternative to visual assessments of ripeness using variables such as firmness and texture. Visual inspection is faster and primarily based on color observation, 9,10 but it is highly dependent on lighting conditions. Conversely, tactile inspection offers precise measurements of mechanical properties but is slower and requires careful fruit manipulation, making it less suitable for fruits with rapid spoilage rates, soft skin, and a tendency to bruise. Insidiously, many fruits soften when ripe and become subject to bruising, making tactile inspection a delicate process that contributes to spoilage.

Fruit inspections are critical for harvesting decisions. Traditionally, these decisions have been made by human workers, leading to challenges such as labor shortages, worker health concerns, and inaccuracies in picking, which exacerbate spoilage during pre- and post-harvesting stages 11-13. In recent years, harvesting robots with integrated inspection capabilities have emerged as a promising technology to reduce spoilage and improve distribution efficiency 14,15. However, most current robotic systems are designed for indoor applications, even though over 99.9% of crops are cultivated in outdoor environments, with greenhouse farming comprising less than 0.1% of global cropland area 16,17. These robots typically use robotic arms and grippers, often integrated into wheeled platforms, with inspection systems based on either visual or tactile sensors.

Vision sensors such as RGBD, CMOS, thermal, and multi-hyper-spectral cameras are employed to gather data and assess fruit ripeness based on color 9,15,18-20. Similarly, tactile sensors, integrated into robotic grippers, often measure changes in deformation through technologies such as conductive elastomers, fabrics, piezoelectric sensors, optical fibers , cameras, metal wires, liquid metals, and carbon nanotubes 21-33. These sensors detect changes in capacitance, resistance, light loss, deformation, or magnetic flux to infer fruit characteristics 31,34- 37.

Current harvesting robots face several challenges when using these sensors. Robotic visual inspections primarily rely on external or head-mounted cameras integrated into robotic arms or platforms38,39. These systems impose significant limitations on visual servoing capabilities due to occlusion, partially hidden objects, and low accuracy in detecting color, size, and shape 40-42. Lighting conditions can also cause detection errors of up to 50% 41. Robotic tactile inspections often use advanced materials such as conductive elastomers, optical fibers, or carbon nanotubes integrated into grippers. These systems, however, face scalability issues, uneven sensor distribution across gripper surfaces, and integration complexities 34, reducing the reliability of measurements and hindering direct physical interaction with fruits 43. Moreover, many robotic systems lack the ability for simultaneous close inspection, as their sensors are often bulky and integrated into rigid grippers, increasing the risk of bruising during pre- and post-harvesting stages 26,38-40.

One method of addressing these challenges fuses sensing capabilities from simultaneous high-resolution visual inspection and distributed tactile feedback. Combining tactile and visual measurements provides a more accurate assessment of ripeness and other characteristics such as shape and size. Soft robotic systems made of elastomeric materials, which inherently enable gentle interaction, permit tactile assessment and picking that addresses bruising issues, improving harvesting decisions, and reducing spoilage caused by inaccurate or time-consuming measurements 44-48.

This integrated approach enhances sensor utility by leveraging each sensor’s strengths to compensate for its limitations, making the technology applicable to a broader range of fruits and environmental conditions. For instance, tactile inputs can verify visual measurements in poor lighting conditions or for unfamiliar fruits, and vice versa. Such advancements can increase the variety of fruits distributed, reduce spoilage, and lower supply chain costs by enabling faster and more accurate harvesting decisions.

To achieve high-resolution visual and tactile measurements for rapid harvesting, integrating a collocated vision system and stretchable optical fibers provides a pathway to develop compact, scalable grasping solutions without complex integration challenges 22,23. Fixed camera approaches are prone to self-occlusion, whereas moving camera collocation addresses this issue, significantly improving visual dexterity and enabling the extraction of high-resolution features. However, moving-camera collocation has primarily been applied in pose estimation and collision avoidance, with limited exploration in fruit ripeness estimation 34,42.

Existing grippers with integrated tactile or vision systems typically focus on a single sensing modality or offer limited multimodal integration49. For instance, most vision systems are primarily designed for object detection but do not provide additional outputs such as shape or size information that is especially useful for tasks like fruit picking50-52. Similarly, grippers are designed only to rely on tactile sensors measurements, which often tend to be bulky relative to the gripper’s size and limited manipulation dexterity34-37,46,47,53-58. This imposition causes design constraints, requiring larger grippers that compromise flexibility and workspace. Beyond vision and tactile, only a few grippers incorporate curvature (proprioceptive) sensors with tactile feedback to estimate the bending state and touch59-66. Even when present, these sensors are typically not integrated with other sensing modules, despite their importance in handling dynamic objects. Moreover, most of these grippers are rigid; only a limited number of soft grippers are capable of achieving embodied multimodal sensing37. Even those are often restricted to tactile feedback, with cameras mounted externally on the main robotic platform rather than directly integrated into the gripper67-69. Enabling true multimodal sensing within a gripper is essential for achieving versatile manipulation capabilities, particularly under dynamic conditions. However, integrating a large and diverse set of sensors into a compact form factor—without compromising the gripper’s functional performance—remains a significant challenge. This becomes even more critical in agricultural tasks, where object characteristics such as shape, size, color, ripeness, and weight can vary substantially. A soft gripper with embedded tactile, vision, and curvature sensors that collectively provide diverse sensing modalities would significantly enhance manipulation performance in such variable environments as exist in biological systems, which have not yet been fully realized into soft grippers.

Previously, we have developed and implemented soft optical fiber-based tactile sensors that measure light intensity loss in response to deformation or force. By implementing these sensors in a manipulator, we were able to demonstrate the prediction of ripeness in fruit (i.e., tomatoes) from tactile perception without vision, but imprecisely .22

We fused low-cost, camera-based vision and fiber-optic-based tactile inspection into a five-digit (radially symmetric) soft gripper featuring underactuated control, rapid actuation, a large workspace, and high load-carrying capacity. It also includes a rotational module for picking fruit by twisting its stem, as well as hosting the control unit. The visual sensing uses a collocated camera and a time-of-flight sensor, enabling high-resolution measurements of shape, size, and color. For curvature sensing, we integrated stretchable fiber optics directly into each finger, while for tactile sensing we used a U-shaped fiber optic at each fingertip. Additionally, we integrated a pressure sensor to enable closed-loop grasping, allowing the gripper to assess both physical and non-physical object characteristics through a multimodal sensing approach.

The gripper is 3D printed, assembled, and then thermally fused into a monolithic structure. For vision sensing, we embedded a miniature Raspberry Pi camera and an IR-based time-of-flight (ToF) sensor into the palm side of the gripper. Similarly, for touch and curvature sensing, we embedded stretchable optical fibers paired with laser diodes and phototransistors into each finger.

We actuated the gripper pneumatically, using solenoid valve actuation and pressure sensor feedback. We developed a custom PCB to read tactile, curvature, ToF, and pressure sensor data while also controlling solenoid valve actuation. We connected the PCB to a Raspberry Pi, running an algorithm that fuses the sensor data to assess the object's state and perform object manipulation and grasping. The harvesting module consists of a 3D-printed planetary gear rotational system, which is integrated with a slip ring and a DC motor. Finally, we mounted the gripper, Raspberry Pi, PCB, and harvesting module onto a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm.

We then characterized the manipulator’s workspace, bending angle, blocking force, pulling force, and load-carrying capacity under varying pressures and time intervals. We validated the bending angle and blocking force measurements through finite element simulations. After quantifying the manipulator’s grasping characteristics, we tested the vision, tactile, and curvature sensors. We evaluated the vision sensor by testing it on objects of six different colors (black, red, blue, green, white, yellow), four different shapes (triangle, circle, quadrilateral, and fruits), and three different sizes (3, 4, 5 cm). We examined the relationship between the finger bending angle, input pressure, and sensor output for the curvature sensors. Finally, we measured the relationship between applied force and tactile sensor output using a compression test on objects of different stiffness.

The gripper is fast, closing its workspace in under two seconds at 80 kPa; strong, lifting to 1 kg (1,600% of its weight) by applying a grasping force of 6 N; and has the ability to expand its enveloping area from 200 mm2 to 14000 mm2 to accommodate large ranges of produce size. Each finger exerted up to 1.5 N and bent up to 240°, closely matching FEA simulations. For vision tests, we identified the hue channel in the HSV color space as most sensitive to changes in ripeness level and more robust to different lighting conditions. The results reveal accurate color detection from our hue-based strategy and 100% shape prediction under fixed lighting at 8 cm, with perimeter measurement errors decreasing as object size increased. The curvature sensor exhibited a sharp light intensity drop to -7 dB beyond the 77.5° critical bending angle, while the tactile sensor effectively distinguished between rigid and soft objects, including strawberries, with light intensity changes of up to -8.91 dB under an applied force of 4 N. We demonstrate the gripper’s manipulation efficacy by picking various objects and fruits in real-time.

---

## Results

2.1. Gripper Design and Working Principle
In Fig. 1, we present a general overview of our work. The objective is to demonstrate our gripper’s design and its multifunctional sensing capabilities. The soft gripper has five fingers arranged radially at 72o intervals. All actuators are connected to a rigid chassis called the finger holder. Each finger actuator has an isosceles trapezoidal form based on the principle of flexible fluidic actuators, featuring interconnected chambers made of soft elastomers. When pressurized by a pneumatic source, the chambers expand and push against each other, causing the finger to bend. A strain-limiting layer on the palmar side controls the bending. All five actuators attach to a pentagonal-shaped finger holder. The holder contains an internal channel that connects each finger’s air source to a single barbed connector, allowing simultaneous actuation of all fingers from one pneumatic input. Furthermore, we designed the rotational module to harvest fruits by rotating the gripper after it grasps the fruit. Continuous rotation about the gripper’s roll axis twists the fruit trusses, allowing the fruit to detach from the peduncle (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Movie 1). The gripper assembly includes both the gripper itself and a rotational module (Fig. 1a). A detailed explanation of the gripper design and the rationale behind its mechanism is provided in sections 4.1 and 4.2 of the Experimental Methods (EM), while the fabrication process is described in Supplementary Fig. 2 and section 1 of the Supporting Information (SI).

In Fig. 1b, we illustrate how tactile and curvature sensors are embedded in the gripper. The red light indicates the curvature sensor, while the blue light indicates the tactile sensor (Supplementary Movie 2). We tested the gripper on two fruits—strawberries and avocados—under different lighting conditions. From our results, we were unable to visually characterize ripeness because measurements were highly influenced by lighting conditions. The tactile feedback, however, was unaffected by lighting changes and accurately measured the ripeness of both fruits (Fig. 1c-i).

2.2. Gripper Characterization
In Fig. 2a–b, we show images of the fingers printed on the build platform, along with the corresponding material properties and stress-strain relationships. The rigid material 𝐸 = 1.7 GPa 𝛾 = 0.3) exhibits a tensile strength of approximately 40 MPa, while the soft material’s (SIL 30, 𝐸 = 1 MPa, 𝛾 = 3.5) tensile strength is about 4 MPa. Fig. 2c–d presents the finger bending angle results and corresponding FEM simulations (Supplementary Movies 3-4). Each finger can bend up to 240° at 70 kPa, which matches the experimental findings. The simulation data indicate a maximum stress of 0.887 MPa and a minimum safety factor of 3.834 at 70 kPa, corresponding to a bending angle of 245.1°. We describe the experimental and simulation procedures in EM sections 4.3 and 4.4.

Fig. 2e–f illustrates the workspace analysis with both visual and simulation representations. The maximum workspace area is around 14,000 mm² at 0 kPa, and the minimum is about 200 mm² at 80 kPa (1,500% of the original area). Images of the gripper at different pressures are superimposed alongside their simulated counterparts (Supplementary Movies 5-6). We describe the experimental procedures in SI section 2 and the simulation procedures in EM section 4.4.

In Fig. 3, we detail the gripper’s force characterization. Fig. 3a–b shows the blocking force exerted by a finger against a rigid object, reaching 1.26 N at 100 kPa. The corresponding simulation at 100 kPa indicates a maximum stress of 0.793 MPa, a minimum safety factor of 4.29, and a blocking force of 1.494 N, aligning well with experimental results (SI section 3 for test procedure, Supplementary Movie 7). Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 3a-c depict the gripper’s pulling force overtime for 4 cm diameter hemispherical objects at input pressures ranging from 70 to 130 kPa. The pulling force increases with input pressure, reaching a maximum of 8.10 N at 130 kPa. Object size also influences pulling force: for a 2 cm diameter hemispherical object, the gripper achieves about 1.63 N at 100 kPa, whereas a 5 cm diameter hemispherical object yields approximately 5.18 N at the same pressure. Overall, larger objects enable higher pulling forces at increased input pressures (see Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 3c, Supplementary Movie 8). Finally, vertical load capacity tests show that the gripper can easily handle up to 1 kg—1,600% of its weight (see Fig. 3e and Supplementary Movie 9). We describe detailed experimental procedures for pulling force, and load capacity tests in SI sections 4 and 5

2.3. Vision sensor characterization
In Fig. 4, we present the characterization of our vision sensor and its accuracy. Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4 show the experimental setup, which includes a studio box for consistent lighting, as well as a gripper, camera, and distance sensor positioned in the same location. Detailed information about this setup and the experimental methods can be found in EM sections 4.5 and 4.6.

We first tested the camera for color measurements. In Fig. 4b, we report the hue distribution of green, red, and strawberry fruit. The results indicate that the mean (µ) and standard deviation (σ) of the hue for the red color is 172.26±25.83, green is 70.77±2.69, and strawberries are 30.01±60.56. We also measured saturation and value distributions (Supplementary Figs. 5-6) for red, green, ripe strawberries, and other colors such as blue, yellow, white, and black. The hue for black proved difficult to measure, while the hues for blue and yellow were about 101.20 ± 1.56 and 17.27±77, respectively. From this analysis, we concluded that hue offers the clearest color differentiation.

We examined strawberries in different ripeness stages: unripe, partially ripe, and fully ripe (labeled strawberry-1, -2, -3, and -4). We observed that the two fully ripe strawberries (strawberry-1 and -2) had hue channel values of 30.01 ±60.56 and 35.45 ±65.93, making them difficult to distinguish from each other due to the large variation in red hue channel values. The partially ripe strawberry (strawberry-3) had a wide hue distribution from 22.44±6.31, while the unripe strawberry (strawberry-4) exhibited a hue is 30.08±4.35. As with the standard color tests, we found that the saturation and value measurements were inconclusive because of constant lighting conditions, whereas the hue channel remained reliable for differentiation.

In Fig. 4c, we present the real-time 2D shape and size estimation of various objects using a collocated camera and distance sensor. We tested standard objects—a cube, sphere, and pyramid of different sizes (3, 4, and 5 cm)—as well as strawberries of various shapes and sizes. The size refers to the characteristic size for each object (diameter for a sphere, edge length for a cube, edge length for a pyramid). See EM section 4.6 for a detailed description of the setup and methodology. Each object was placed at distances of 8, 10, or 12 cm from the camera, and its 2D shape was identified as a quadrilateral, circle, triangle, or random shape, depending on its actual form. Our results demonstrate a ~100% success rate with 95% Wilson confidence intervals (CI) of [0.57,1.00], where n=5 for shape detection at all tested distances (see Supplementary Fig. 7).

We also measured the size of these objects with high accuracy. Fig. 4d shows the measured perimeters for the standard objects and three strawberries. Among these, 3 cm diameter circular objects and strawberries showed the highest mean absolute percentage error (MAPE), at 8% and 10%, respectively. However, the MAPE decreased for larger objects, dropping below 1.8% for cubes at 8 cm (see Fig. 4e). We provide all estimated shape and size data in Supplementary Figs. 7–11, including both masked and real images of the objects.

2.4. Curvature sensor
Curvature sensors are a type of proprioceptive sensor that combines pressure data and bending data. These sensors serve two main purposes: (1) providing bending state information that complement tactile measurements, and (2) enabling load estimation and slip detection. However, the primary function is to monitor the bending state of each finger during grasping. This feedback is essential because it is an underactuated system where all fingers are actuated simultaneously. Curvature sensing allows us to confirm that each finger bends sufficiently to establish stable contact and apply the required force without damaging the fruit.

In Fig. 5a, we present a fully integrated optical fiber sensor embedded in a gripper’s finger, along with an image illustrating red light traveling through the optical fiber from the transmission end (red LED) to the receiver (phototransistor). We designed the finger actuator to function as a curvature sensor. We created a U-shaped channel measuring 0.8 mm in diameter on the palmar side of the finger cover and installed 23 soft clamps to secure the fiber along this channel. The sensor design and characterization procedures are described in EM section 4.7 and SI section 6.

In Fig. 5b, we report the total light received at the phototransistor's end, expressed as voltage output over time at various bending angles. Fig. 5c displays a superimposed image of the gripper with the integrated light guide, highlighting its corresponding bending angles at different applied pressures. We converted the voltage output data into light intensity loss (dB) using Beer-Lambert’s Law, as represented by the following equation22:
Light Intensity Loss (dB) = 10×log 10 (V0/V)

The curvature sensor results indicate that light intensity initially increased from 3.58 dB to 5.09 dB as the bending angle increased from 0° to 77.47°. The bending, however, continued from 77.47° to 211°, and the light intensity dropped to -7 dB, suggesting a critical bending angle for sensor measurements. Fig. 5d plots bending angles against their corresponding light intensity variations at different input pressures. The initial increase in light loss can be explained by our sensor assembly process. While integrating the fibers into the finger, there is micro-bending between the fibers and the clamps, due to minimal compressive loading. This slight bending produces a characteristic response during finger bending at small bends, the stress relaxes, the bends straighten, and the optical signal changes gradually, whereas beyond a critical angle (~75–80°) the fibers enter tensile stretch, and the light intensity decreases sharply. However, the raw data are non-monotonic, which can be compensated by normalizing the light-loss signal with the gripper’s internal pressure (Fig. 5d). This normalization transforms the response into a monotonic relationship that can be directly interpreted as bending angle versus normalized light loss (see Supplementary Fig. 12). Additionally, we demonstrated that the curvature sensor can be used for load capacity estimation and slip detection. We integrated this sensor into the gripper and tested it by holding various loads (200 g, 400 g, and 600 g) at different pressures (70, 80, and 90 kPa). The results showed that the light intensity dropped by 50% when holding 600 g compared to 200 g, effectively capturing load variations. Furthermore, the sensor successfully detected instances of weight slipping, demonstrating its capability to not only sense bending but also detect grasping failures (Fig. 5e). This capability also allowed detection of slipping events during heavy or unstable grasps. While the present study focuses on demonstrating integrated sensing, we envision applying this capability in future automated harvesting systems to sort fruit into weight categories (light, average, heavy).

## Methods

4.1. Gripper design and fabrication
The dimensions of gripper components are as follows: the finger actuator has bases measuring 21.85 mm and 10 mm, legs of 52.83 mm, and a height of 12 mm. The finger holder has a pentagonal shape, with each side measuring 22.35 mm and a height of 20.75 mm. Each face of the holder features a rectangular cavity measuring 11 mm by 8.95 mm by 5.65 mm, with an inlet tube for attaching the actuators. The holder also includes a slot for a camera and a ToF sensor, along with additional slots for the laser diode and phototransistor mounts (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1).

To fabricate the gripper, we used a multi-step process. First, we designed 3D models of the finger actuators, the holder, and other components in SolidWorks 2022 (SolidWorks corps). To simplify printing, each finger actuator was split into two parts: a finger cover and a finger body. In contrast, the finger holder was designed as a single piece. Next, we printed the components on a high-resolution DLS printer (Carbon M1, Carbon Inc.). Finally, we assembled the printed parts using thermal baking (see SI Section 1 for details) and fastening methods such as adhesive bonding, screws, and nuts.

The gripper construction follows a multi-material approach, combining both soft and rigid components. Each finger is made of a soft silicone-polyurethane elastomer (SIL 30, 𝐸 = 1 MPa, 𝛾 = 3.50). The finger holder chassis, tube connectors, camera, ToF sensor, and laser diode 𝐸 =1.7 𝛾 =0.3). Details of the printing protocols are provided in SI section 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2.

4.2. Rotational module design and fabrication
The rotational module relies on gripper rotation about its roll axis. However, this axial rotation also twists the sensor wiring, power supply cables, and pneumatic tubes. To prevent these twists, we divided the rotational module into two parts: a fixed part attached to the gripper end effector and a rotating part that connects the gripper to the control unit. We used planetary gear-based rotational joints to link these parts. We also created a hollow central axis and integrated a concentric slip ring, allowing wires and the pneumatic tube to pass through freely, ensuring a secure connection between the gripper and control unit without twisting.

A high-torque DC gear motor powers the gear transmission, which consists of a spur gear and a pinion. The pinion is fixed to the rotating section, while a floating spur gear connects to the DC motor. We incorporated ball bearings to enable smooth rotation and minimize eccentricity45. We mounted the control unit on the outer perimeter of the rotating part and controlled the DC motor with a double-pole double-throw (DPDT) switch (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Movie 1). We used the same 3D printer to fabricate most of the rotational and fixed sections, along with the gears, connectors, and bolts. We printed these components using rigid polyurethane, the same material used for the finger holder. For assembly, we employed a traditional method using screws and bolts. The detailed printing protocol is discussed in SI section 1.

4.3. Finger bending characterization
We printed a finger actuator with an integrated rigid body to house the laser diode, phototransistor, and pneumatic tube connectors (see Fig. 2d). We then secured the rigid body to a table using a bench vise. To track the bending angle, we placed grid paper behind the actuator and marked the finger with permanent markers. We positioned a tripod-mounted mobile phone camera (with at least 10 megapixels (MP) resolution) at a fixed distance from the finger actuator, ensuring consistent focus and preventing any camera movement during the experiment. We measured the bending angle of the finger actuator at pressure inputs ranging from 0.1 to 1 bar, in increments of 0.1 bar. We used a constant air source with a pressure regulator to maintain a stable air supply. For each pressure setting, we held the pressure for 60 seconds to achieve quasi-static conditions before taking a photograph of the actuator. Afterward, we imported the images into ImageJ, an open-source software, to determine the relationship between bending angle and pressure. We present all results in Section 2.

4.4. Finite element method simulation
We used Ansys 2022 software to conduct finite element simulations and assess the mechanical feasibility of a soft robotic gripper. Our simulations analyzed bending angles, blocking force, and overall gripper response. We examined total displacement (mm), total strain (mm/mm), and equivalent von Mises stress (MPa) for both individual fingers and the entire gripper. To develop the simulation model, we imported SolidWorks files into Ansys Workbench 20.1 and applied the Static Structural module. We added custom material properties to the Ansys material library using elastomer stress-strain data obtained from standard tensile testing (ASTM D412, Die C, 500 mm/min). After fitting the experimental data into a hyperelastic model, we found that the Yeoh 3rd order model provided the best fit, with the following coefficients: C10 = 167,499.9 Pa, C20 = 453.53 Pa, and C30 = 5.5374 Pa. For meshing, we applied a 1 mm nonlinear quadratic mesh, generating 54,514 nodes and 32,908 elements. We set gravity as a body force in all simulations. To simulate the blocking force, we introduced a fixed surface to measure the actuator’s force output. We set contact stiffness for both self-contact and the fixed surface to 200 N/mm³ using the pure penalty method, allowing a penetration of approximately 0.1 µm. We performed nonlinear simulations using the Newton-Raphson method on a 12th Gen Intel(R) Core™ i7-12650H CPU with 64 GB RAM. The bending angle simulation took 17 minutes and 38 seconds, requiring 298 iterations to converge, while the blocking force simulation took 36 minutes and 7 seconds, completing 738 iterations.

4.5. Vision sensor design and fabrication
The vision sensor consists of an RGB camera and a ToF sensor system, built in a collocated configuration. We built a sensor mount that attaches to the center of the palmar side of the finger holder, positioning the sensors side by side in the center of the gripper. These sensors are securely fixed and move with the gripper. For vision, we used a commercial Raspberry Pi camera with a 5-megapixel Arducam 1/4-inch Omnivision OV5647 sensor, featuring a fixed-focus lens, a 160° field of view, and a frame rate of 30 fps, suitable for Raspberry Pi 4 B. For depth sensing, we integrated a ToF Laser Range Finder with a 940 nm laser detector (VL53L0X) capable of measuring distances up to 2 meters. Both sensors were purchased from Amazon.com. To integrate these sensors, we designed a custom slot that holds them securely through a tight fit (see Supplementary Fig. 4). We fixed the entire mount, including the sensors, using through-holes in the finger holder and double-sided tape.

4.6. Vision sensor test
To test the vision sensor, we built a dedicated setup. First, we mounted both the camera and the ToF sensor on the soft gripper to replicate real testing conditions, then attached the gripper to a 3D-printed stand (PLA, Ultimaker 4). We 3D-printed three standard shapes—a cube, a sphere, and a pyramid—and used three different strawberries. To ensure consistent lighting, we used an Amazon studio box with white light (~832 Lux) and a scissor lift stand to adjust the height of the objects for vision measurements. We used Dr. Meter Lx11330B for light measurements. See Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4 for an overview of the setup.

Color: We used cubes (side length = 5 cm) and attached stickers with six different colors (white, black, red, blue, yellow, and green) to evaluate the camera’s color detection algorithm. Each cube was placed on a scissor lift at a fixed distance of 8 cm from the camera, and measurements were taken (Supplementary Table 1). For color detection, we recorded Hue, Saturation, and Value (HSV) data and plotted them in a histogram with probability mass functions. The Hue range was 0 to 180, while Saturation and Value ranged from 0 to 255. We repeated this procedure for all six colors, and the results are presented in Fig. 4b-e and Supplementary Figs. 5-7.

Size estimation: For the size estimation test, we used the same vision sensor setup as in the color detection test. We tested 12 distinct objects with four different shapes: a triangular pyramid, a sphere, a cube, and a strawberry. The triangular pyramids had three different edge lengths (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm), the spheres had three different diameters (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm), and the cubes had three different side lengths (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm). The strawberries varied in size. Each object was placed on a scissor lift, and its outer perimeter was estimated using image data and ToF sensor readings at three distances (8 cm, 10 cm, and 12 cm). To estimate the true object size, we required two pieces of information: (1) the camera’s focal length and (2) the object’s perimeter in the image domain. We calibrated the camera under a pinhole model by placing a cube of known size at various distances and then applied the pinhole method with similar triangle techniques to calculate the actual object size:
f = (dk * v) / h
Where is f the focal length, d is the distance of the object along the principal axis, v is the number of vertical pixels on the square target object, h is the true height of the object.

To ensure the accuracy of ToF sensor measurements, we calibrated the sensor by comparing its readings with objects at known distances. We used this data to develop a calibration curve that mapped the ToF sensor measurements to actual distances and then integrated it into the size estimation code. Additionally, we ensured that the camera and ToF sensor were properly aligned so their coordinate frames coincided (i.e., the camera’s principal axis was aligned with the ToF sensor). This alignment guaranteed that the ToF sensor provided the correct distance between the camera and the object for every measurement.

We also applied temporal smoothing to improve size estimation accuracy across multiple frames. We used a receding horizon filter with a window size of 20 frames, pushing each new size estimate into a queue and dropping the oldest estimate. Several consistency checks (e.g., a shape test and a size percentage error test) were performed before adding any data point to the queue. The output size estimate was then calculated as the average of the 20-frame window (Supplementary Table 2).

Shape estimation: For the shape estimation, we kept the same setup as the previous experiments, except that the objects’ sizes were kept at 4cm. We used triangular pyramids, spheres, cubes, and strawberries for the shape estimate. We only measured the 2D geometry for shape detection, so triangular pyramids were classified as triangles, spheres were classified as circles, and cubes were classified as quadrilaterals (Supplementary Table 3). Strawberries were classified as unknown. The results are presented in Fig. 4b-e and Supplementary Figs. 5-7.

4.7. Tactile and curvature sensor design and fabrication
We used a 0.7 mm stretchable, clear thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) fiber from Crystal Tec Korea (purchased via Amazon). We connected both ends of the fiber to the laser diode and phototransistor mounts. Each mount is cylindrical, with an outer diameter of 5.5 mm, an inner diameter of 3.1 mm, and a 0.8 mm fiber holder. We placed and glued these mounts into slots on the finger holder. Furthermore, for the light emitter, we employed a 3 mm laser infrared diode (1.5 mW, 850 nm), and for the receiver, we used a phototransistor with a spectral response of 450–1080 nm (purchased from digkey.com). When the finger bends, it deforms the fiber, that changes the light intensity. We measure this light intensity variation as a voltage output.

We designed the tactile sensor as a modular, U-shaped conduit—2 mm thick and 10 mm wide—composed of both soft and rigid materials (Fig. 6a). The base conduit is rigid and houses the diode and phototransistor mounts, as well as the fiber. The second layer (the contact layer) is soft and features a 0.8 mm diameter channel with 19 integrated soft clamps along the conduit. We used the same mount dimensions and light components (laser diode and phototransistor) as in the curvature sensors (Fig. 6a).

To fabricate the tactile sensors, we first 3D-printed a rigid polyurethane structure (RPU70) measuring 1.25 mm in thickness, followed by a 0.75 mm silicone urethane layer (SIL30) containing the channel and clamps. We joined these layers using wet resin and then baked them in an oven (see SI section 1 for printing procedure details). Next, we threaded the TPU fiber through the conduit channel, installed the fibers, laser diode, and phototransistor, and finally mounted the completed sensor onto the fingers. We used Black Panther™ 85 (𝐸 = 4.83 MPa, 𝛾 = 1.21) as a detachable adhesive to attach the tactile sensors to the fingertips (Fig. 6b).

The optical fibers for both curvature and tactile sensor are bonded into rigid holders, and the holders are bonded to the fingers, so the relative geometry is fixed during operation. The light source and photodetector (LED and phototransistor) are rigidly mounted to the holder and encapsulated with an opaque silicone sealant, that blocks stray light and further stiffens the source–fiber and fiber–detector interfaces against vibration or shift. Additionally, emitting/detecting elements are enclosed and spectrally separated from typical ambient illumination, the sensor output is largely insensitive to room lighting.

4.8. Tactile sensor characterization
We built and characterized five tactile sensors before integrating them into the gripper. EM section 4.1 provides further details on the design and fabrication of these sensors. We powered each sensor’s laser diode and phototransistor using the same circuit from the curvature sensor tests and recorded the phototransistor’s voltage output through an Arduino Uno. Because the sensor is U-shaped, it offers two contact faces (top and side), so we tested both faces independently for each sensor.

We interpret the sensor’s output as a voltage change, which corresponds to deformation and light intensity loss. However, effective tactile feedback requires both force and displacement information, so we also correlated the force output with the voltage change at a given displacement. To perform this task, we used a micro universal testing machine (maximum 10 N load cell; Cell Scale) to apply a compressive load on the sensor while measuring force, displacement, and voltage. We attached each sensor to the machine's moving shaft with a custom 3D-printed fixture that allows both orientations of the sensor to be tested. We ensured that each sensor face and the object remained perfectly parallel (see Supplementary Fig. 13a-b for the setup).

We tested the sensors against four types of materials: an extra soft material (Ecoflex 10, Shore 00-10, E = 55.2 kPa at =1.0), a soft material (Dragon Skin 10, Shore 10A, 𝐸 = 152 kPa, 𝛾 = 1.0), a rigid material (RPU 70, Shore 80D, 𝐸 = 1.7 GPa, 𝛾 = 0.3), and actual strawberries. We molded the extra soft and soft materials into semispherical shapes and 3D-printed a rigid semispherical shape in PLA (Ultimaker). For each sensor face, we zeroed the load cell, positioned the sensor to barely touch the object, and applied a 0.7 mm displacement under displacement control. We ran seven compression tests per material, sampling force, displacement, and voltage data at 10 Hz. We also captured images at 1 Hz using the testing machine’s integrated camera. We repeated these tests for both faces of all five sensors and presented the results in section 2 and Fig. 6e-g, Supplementary Fig. 13c-d, Supplementary Figs. 14-18.

4.9. Control unit design and fabrication
We designed the gripper’s control unit around a Raspberry Pi to manage inputs from 13 sensors and two solenoid valves. The 13 sensors include one camera, five analog tactile sensors, five analog curvature sensors, one analog pressure sensor, and one digital ToF sensor that communicates via the I²C protocol. We used two digital outputs to control the valves, which brought the total I/O signals to over 70 wires. To handle these connections efficiently, we developed a custom printed circuit board (PCB) that interfaces the gripper’s I/O signals with the Raspberry Pi.

Because the Raspberry Pi only supports digital communication protocols (I²C, SPI, and UART), we used three high-resolution 16-bit analog-to-digital converters (Adafruit ADS1115) to read the 11 analog sensors and transmit their data to the Raspberry Pi via I²C. We also added an I²C port on the PCB for the ToF sensor. To drive the valves, we used two Raspberry Pi GPIO pins connected to a motor driver (1.2 A, 12 V Pololu 8833), which we integrated into the PCB alongside the two solenoid valves. Finally, we linked the PCB to the Raspberry Pi with jumper wires.

The valves require more current than the Raspberry Pi can supply, so we powered them from an external source (bench power supply). We also used an external uninterruptible power supply (UPS, 5 V output, 1A max) for the Raspberry Pi. We routed power from both the UPS and the external supply through a slip ring before delivering it to the Pi and solenoid valves. To accommodate this, we modified a USB-C cable for the Raspberry Pi connection. Supplementary Figs. 19-23 present the complete diagram and circuit design.

4.10. Robot arm control code
For the robot arm, we used the M320 Cobot robot. We took advantage of its built-in drag-and-teach functionality to write a Python script that allowed us to plan the robot’s trajectory. The drag-and-teach feature lets you program a path by physically moving the robot through a series of waypoints. After starting this script in the command prompt, we moved the robot through the desired set of waypoints using manual control by human operators, which were recorded and saved in a JSON file. Once the waypoints were created, we wrote another script to iterate through them, directing the robot to move to each waypoint, pause for a set period, and then continue to the next waypoint. This script would loop indefinitely unless it was halted, ensuring the robot would continuously execute this path (see Supplementary Fig. 23).

Using these scripts, we programmed the four-step path that the robot would follow during the integrated test (not picking fruits directly on the plant). Each test began with the robot in its default position, with the arm extended straight up (State A). From there, the robot moved to a position where the gripper’s camera faced directly downward over the object (State B). Next, the robot moved straight down so the gripper contacted the object (State C). Finally, the robot moved to an intermediate position away from the object (State D). The robot repeated this sequence from State A through State D for each test (see Table 1: Algorithm 1).

Gripper Control Code: The onboard Raspberry Pi was responsible for collecting all the vision and tactile data from the gripper. We developed a single Python script that handled all data collection. The script consists of two main parts: the vision code and the grasping code.

Vision Code: The vision code was the first part of the Python script, running whenever the script was called. It activated the camera and used a computer vision algorithm (OpenCV) to detect objects within the camera’s field of view (FOV). See Supplementary Tables 1-3: Algorithms 2-4 for a detailed description of the algorithm. The script saved an RGB image of the detected object with a bounding box around it, separate HSV histogram files in image format, and a segmented image of the object printed with shape and size information.

Grasping Code: The gripper control code was the second part of the Python script, running immediately after the vision code finished. It collected data from five curvatures and five tactile sensors (as voltage outputs), as well as the gripper’s pressure and the time elapsed. Once activated, it triggered the solenoids to allow air from the air compressor into the gripper. As the gripper inflated, the onboard pressure sensor monitored the pressure. When the gripper reached the desired pressure, the solenoids were closed, maintaining the pressure without releasing air.

4.11. Integrated robot arm and gripper test

The integrated test includes full-scale robot arm manipulation and real-time measurements of various objects. For the integrated test, we mounted the robot arm on a workbench using clamps. We placed the objects on a separate table next to the workbench with a brown-colored background to create a sharp contrast between the objects and the background. We placed the object on a scissor lift so we could adjust its height and ensure it remained within the robot arm’s workspace. In Line 236, which value did author mean: ”the saturation and value...” ? The intensity

generally exhibits greater variability than saturation or value due to its mathematical dependence
on the relative ratios of the RGB channels. Different colors will cause very different hue values.
In contrast, saturation is defined by the relative difference between the maximum and minimum
channel intensities and value is defined as the maximum channel intensity. Under constant lighting,

We would like to thank reviewer 2 for the comprehensive review and feedback for our paper. We

The authors present a soft pneumatic gripper with integrated proprioceptive and tactile
sensing. By combining these capabilities with vision, the gripper can assess fruit ripeness and

Author Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback. To contextualize our

1) that contrasts prior soft grippers and our system in terms of the number of embedded
sensors, the sensing modalities integrated, and the resulting capabilities.

autonomous, human-triggered picking, our next step is a fully autonomous control

the readout therefore represents a spatially averaged normal load over the contact patch.

outermost tip locations; the area is then A=πr2. The maximum workspace corresponds to

9. Fig. 3d is confusing to read at first glance. I suggest using different colors to indicate the

manuscript.

Author’s Response: We have added explicit definitions to the revised manuscript. In this

## Paper

## Abstract

Modern agricultural robotic systems are constrained by limited sensing and manipulation capabilities, particularly in fruit harvesting, where variability in color, size, and firmness poses significant challenges. Existing solutions, often reliant on rigid grippers and single-modality sensors, frequently cause fruit bruising and substantial post-harvest losses. Here, we present a compact, five-finger soft robotic gripper with integrated multimodal sensing—including vision, tactile, and curvature sensing—for adaptive and non-destructive fruit harvesting. The system incorporates 13 sensors, onboard electronics, local computation, and a rotational harvesting module. Each finger embeds custom stretchable optical fibers functioning as tactile and curvature sensors, while the palm houses a miniaturized camera and distance sensor. The gripper actuates within two seconds at 80 kPa, exerts up to 6 N of pulling force, and lifts objects up to 1 kg—more than 16 times its own weight. Its workspace expands from 200 mm² to 14,000 mm², enabling the handling of fruits with diverse shapes and sizes. Each finger bends up to 240°, with performance closely matching finite element predictions. For vision measurements, the hue channel in the HSV color space enables robust real-time color detection, achieving 100% shape classification accuracy and a size measurement error below 1.8%. Tactile sensors distinguish soft from firm objects, while curvature sensors accurately measure the finger’s bending state—both based on optical signal loss. Real-time demonstrations validate the system’s ability to assess ripeness using multimodal data (vision, tactile, and curvature) and successfully harvest greenhouse strawberries with minimal damage. This platform offers a versatile, sensor-rich solution for both precision agriculture and general-purpose robotic manipulation.

---

## Introduction

Many fruits ripen at varying rates and are primarily inspected visually, relying on changes in skin color to determine optimal picking times for farm-to-market distribution. Some crops have acceptable quality for commercial harvest over a period of weeks (e.g., citrus), whereas others must be harvested within a day or two of achieving acceptable quality (e.g., strawberries, raspberries). Fruit harvested too early will not have good flavor and sweetness, whereas fruit harvested after the peak of ripeness may be too soft and spoil quickly. 1-4. Fruits that develop over a long period (e.g., pomegranate, citrus) are typically firmer, often have thicker skin, and are easier to inspect visually due to their slower spoilage rates. In contrast, fruits with shorter ripening periods (e.g., berries) are usually soft, often have thinner skin, and are more challenging to inspect visually because of their rapid transition from acceptable quality to spoilage. These differences contribute to substantial variation in postharvest losses in the supply chain, with approximately 6–7% loss for pomegranates and up to 25% for strawberries 4-7.

Visual assessment of fruit quality is not always feasible, as many fruits exhibit minimal or inconsistent changes in skin color that may not be associated with ripeness. For example, avocados and pawpaws do not reliably change from a green skin color during ripening and vary in ripening time. Avocados can be of an acceptable quality for harvest over a period of weeks, whereas pawpaws become too soft in days after they ripen, leading to high spoilage rates during distribution. Postharvest losses of avocados can reach up to 24% 8, and pawpaws, despite being delicious, are only distributed locally because of their short storage life and ease of bruising.

Tactile inspections are an alternative to visual assessments of ripeness using variables such as firmness and texture. Visual inspection is faster and primarily based on color observation, 9,10 but it is highly dependent on lighting conditions. Conversely, tactile inspection offers precise measurements of mechanical properties but is slower and requires careful fruit manipulation, making it less suitable for fruits with rapid spoilage rates, soft skin, and a tendency to bruise. Insidiously, many fruits soften when ripe and become subject to bruising, making tactile inspection a delicate process that contributes to spoilage.

Fruit inspections are critical for harvesting decisions. Traditionally, these decisions have been made by human workers, leading to challenges such as labor shortages, worker health concerns, and inaccuracies in picking, which exacerbate spoilage during pre- and post-harvesting stages 11-13. In recent years, harvesting robots with integrated inspection capabilities have emerged as a promising technology to reduce spoilage and improve distribution efficiency 14,15. However, most current robotic systems are designed for indoor applications, even though over 99.9% of crops are cultivated in outdoor environments, with greenhouse farming comprising less than 0.1% of global cropland area 16,17. These robots typically use robotic arms and grippers, often integrated into wheeled platforms, with inspection systems based on either visual or tactile sensors.

Vision sensors such as RGBD, CMOS, thermal, and multi-hyper-spectral cameras are employed to gather data and assess fruit ripeness based on color 9,15,18-20. Similarly, tactile sensors, integrated into robotic grippers, often measure changes in deformation through technologies such as conductive elastomers, fabrics, piezoelectric sensors, optical fibers , cameras, metal wires, liquid metals, and carbon nanotubes 21-33. These sensors detect changes in capacitance, resistance, light loss, deformation, or magnetic flux to infer fruit characteristics 31,34- 37.

Current harvesting robots face several challenges when using these sensors. Robotic visual inspections primarily rely on external or head-mounted cameras integrated into robotic arms or platforms38,39. These systems impose significant limitations on visual servoing capabilities due to occlusion, partially hidden objects, and low accuracy in detecting color, size, and shape 40-42. Lighting conditions can also cause detection errors of up to 50% 41. Robotic tactile inspections often use advanced materials such as conductive elastomers, optical fibers, or carbon nanotubes integrated into grippers. These systems, however, face scalability issues, uneven sensor distribution across gripper surfaces, and integration complexities 34, reducing the reliability of measurements and hindering direct physical interaction with fruits 43. Moreover, many robotic systems lack the ability for simultaneous close inspection, as their sensors are often bulky and integrated into rigid grippers, increasing the risk of bruising during pre- and post-harvesting stages 26,38-40.

One method of addressing these challenges fuses sensing capabilities from simultaneous high-resolution visual inspection and distributed tactile feedback. Combining tactile and visual measurements provides a more accurate assessment of ripeness and other characteristics such as shape and size. Soft robotic systems made of elastomeric materials, which inherently enable gentle interaction, permit tactile assessment and picking that addresses bruising issues, improving harvesting decisions, and reducing spoilage caused by inaccurate or time-consuming measurements 44-48.

This integrated approach enhances sensor utility by leveraging each sensor’s strengths to compensate for its limitations, making the technology applicable to a broader range of fruits and environmental conditions. For instance, tactile inputs can verify visual measurements in poor lighting conditions or for unfamiliar fruits, and vice versa. Such advancements can increase the variety of fruits distributed, reduce spoilage, and lower supply chain costs by enabling faster and more accurate harvesting decisions.

To achieve high-resolution visual and tactile measurements for rapid harvesting, integrating a collocated vision system and stretchable optical fibers provides a pathway to develop compact, scalable grasping solutions without complex integration challenges 22,23. Fixed camera approaches are prone to self-occlusion, whereas moving camera collocation addresses this issue, significantly improving visual dexterity and enabling the extraction of high-resolution features. However, moving-camera collocation has primarily been applied in pose estimation and collision avoidance, with limited exploration in fruit ripeness estimation 34,42.

Existing grippers with integrated tactile or vision systems typically focus on a single sensing modality or offer limited multimodal integration49. For instance, most vision systems are primarily designed for object detection but do not provide additional outputs such as shape or size information that is especially useful for tasks like fruit picking50-52. Similarly, grippers are designed only to rely on tactile sensors measurements, which often tend to be bulky relative to the gripper’s size and limited manipulation dexterity34-37,46,47,53-58. This imposition causes design constraints, requiring larger grippers that compromise flexibility and workspace. Beyond vision and tactile, only a few grippers incorporate curvature (proprioceptive) sensors with tactile feedback to estimate the bending state and touch59-66. Even when present, these sensors are typically not integrated with other sensing modules, despite their importance in handling dynamic objects. Moreover, most of these grippers are rigid; only a limited number of soft grippers are capable of achieving embodied multimodal sensing37. Even those are often restricted to tactile feedback, with cameras mounted externally on the main robotic platform rather than directly integrated into the gripper67-69. Enabling true multimodal sensing within a gripper is essential for achieving versatile manipulation capabilities, particularly under dynamic conditions. However, integrating a large and diverse set of sensors into a compact form factor—without compromising the gripper’s functional performance—remains a significant challenge. This becomes even more critical in agricultural tasks, where object characteristics such as shape, size, color, ripeness, and weight can vary substantially. A soft gripper with embedded tactile, vision, and curvature sensors that collectively provide diverse sensing modalities would significantly enhance manipulation performance in such variable environments as exist in biological systems, which have not yet been fully realized into soft grippers.

Previously, we have developed and implemented soft optical fiber-based tactile sensors that measure light intensity loss in response to deformation or force. By implementing these sensors in a manipulator, we were able to demonstrate the prediction of ripeness in fruit (i.e., tomatoes) from tactile perception without vision, but imprecisely .22

We fused low-cost, camera-based vision and fiber-optic-based tactile inspection into a five-digit (radially symmetric) soft gripper featuring underactuated control, rapid actuation, a large workspace, and high load-carrying capacity. It also includes a rotational module for picking fruit by twisting its stem, as well as hosting the control unit. The visual sensing uses a collocated camera and a time-of-flight sensor, enabling high-resolution measurements of shape, size, and color. For curvature sensing, we integrated stretchable fiber optics directly into each finger, while for tactile sensing we used a U-shaped fiber optic at each fingertip. Additionally, we integrated a pressure sensor to enable closed-loop grasping, allowing the gripper to assess both physical and non-physical object characteristics through a multimodal sensing approach.

The gripper is 3D printed, assembled, and then thermally fused into a monolithic structure. For vision sensing, we embedded a miniature Raspberry Pi camera and an IR-based time-of-flight (ToF) sensor into the palm side of the gripper. Similarly, for touch and curvature sensing, we embedded stretchable optical fibers paired with laser diodes and phototransistors into each finger.

We actuated the gripper pneumatically, using solenoid valve actuation and pressure sensor feedback. We developed a custom PCB to read tactile, curvature, ToF, and pressure sensor data while also controlling solenoid valve actuation. We connected the PCB to a Raspberry Pi, running an algorithm that fuses the sensor data to assess the object's state and perform object manipulation and grasping. The harvesting module consists of a 3D-printed planetary gear rotational system, which is integrated with a slip ring and a DC motor. Finally, we mounted the gripper, Raspberry Pi, PCB, and harvesting module onto a six-degree-of-freedom (DOF) robotic arm.

We then characterized the manipulator’s workspace, bending angle, blocking force, pulling force, and load-carrying capacity under varying pressures and time intervals. We validated the bending angle and blocking force measurements through finite element simulations. After quantifying the manipulator’s grasping characteristics, we tested the vision, tactile, and curvature sensors. We evaluated the vision sensor by testing it on objects of six different colors (black, red, blue, green, white, yellow), four different shapes (triangle, circle, quadrilateral, and fruits), and three different sizes (3, 4, 5 cm). We examined the relationship between the finger bending angle, input pressure, and sensor output for the curvature sensors. Finally, we measured the relationship between applied force and tactile sensor output using a compression test on objects of different stiffness.

The gripper is fast, closing its workspace in under two seconds at 80 kPa; strong, lifting to 1 kg (1,600% of its weight) by applying a grasping force of 6 N; and has the ability to expand its enveloping area from 200 mm2 to 14000 mm2 to accommodate large ranges of produce size. Each finger exerted up to 1.5 N and bent up to 240°, closely matching FEA simulations. For vision tests, we identified the hue channel in the HSV color space as most sensitive to changes in ripeness level and more robust to different lighting conditions. The results reveal accurate color detection from our hue-based strategy and 100% shape prediction under fixed lighting at 8 cm, with perimeter measurement errors decreasing as object size increased. The curvature sensor exhibited a sharp light intensity drop to -7 dB beyond the 77.5° critical bending angle, while the tactile sensor effectively distinguished between rigid and soft objects, including strawberries, with light intensity changes of up to -8.91 dB under an applied force of 4 N. We demonstrate the gripper’s manipulation efficacy by picking various objects and fruits in real-time.

---

## Results

2.1. Gripper Design and Working Principle
In Fig. 1, we present a general overview of our work. The objective is to demonstrate our gripper’s design and its multifunctional sensing capabilities. The soft gripper has five fingers arranged radially at 72o intervals. All actuators are connected to a rigid chassis called the finger holder. Each finger actuator has an isosceles trapezoidal form based on the principle of flexible fluidic actuators, featuring interconnected chambers made of soft elastomers. When pressurized by a pneumatic source, the chambers expand and push against each other, causing the finger to bend. A strain-limiting layer on the palmar side controls the bending. All five actuators attach to a pentagonal-shaped finger holder. The holder contains an internal channel that connects each finger’s air source to a single barbed connector, allowing simultaneous actuation of all fingers from one pneumatic input. Furthermore, we designed the rotational module to harvest fruits by rotating the gripper after it grasps the fruit. Continuous rotation about the gripper’s roll axis twists the fruit trusses, allowing the fruit to detach from the peduncle (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Movie 1). The gripper assembly includes both the gripper itself and a rotational module (Fig. 1a). A detailed explanation of the gripper design and the rationale behind its mechanism is provided in sections 4.1 and 4.2 of the Experimental Methods (EM), while the fabrication process is described in Supplementary Fig. 2 and section 1 of the Supporting Information (SI).

In Fig. 1b, we illustrate how tactile and curvature sensors are embedded in the gripper. The red light indicates the curvature sensor, while the blue light indicates the tactile sensor (Supplementary Movie 2). We tested the gripper on two fruits—strawberries and avocados—under different lighting conditions. From our results, we were unable to visually characterize ripeness because measurements were highly influenced by lighting conditions. The tactile feedback, however, was unaffected by lighting changes and accurately measured the ripeness of both fruits (Fig. 1c-i).

2.2. Gripper Characterization
In Fig. 2a–b, we show images of the fingers printed on the build platform, along with the corresponding material properties and stress-strain relationships. The rigid material 𝐸 = 1.7 GPa 𝛾 = 0.3) exhibits a tensile strength of approximately 40 MPa, while the soft material’s (SIL 30, 𝐸 = 1 MPa, 𝛾 = 3.5) tensile strength is about 4 MPa. Fig. 2c–d presents the finger bending angle results and corresponding FEM simulations (Supplementary Movies 3-4). Each finger can bend up to 240° at 70 kPa, which matches the experimental findings. The simulation data indicate a maximum stress of 0.887 MPa and a minimum safety factor of 3.834 at 70 kPa, corresponding to a bending angle of 245.1°. We describe the experimental and simulation procedures in EM sections 4.3 and 4.4.

Fig. 2e–f illustrates the workspace analysis with both visual and simulation representations. The maximum workspace area is around 14,000 mm² at 0 kPa, and the minimum is about 200 mm² at 80 kPa (1,500% of the original area). Images of the gripper at different pressures are superimposed alongside their simulated counterparts (Supplementary Movies 5-6). We describe the experimental procedures in SI section 2 and the simulation procedures in EM section 4.4.

In Fig. 3, we detail the gripper’s force characterization. Fig. 3a–b shows the blocking force exerted by a finger against a rigid object, reaching 1.26 N at 100 kPa. The corresponding simulation at 100 kPa indicates a maximum stress of 0.793 MPa, a minimum safety factor of 4.29, and a blocking force of 1.494 N, aligning well with experimental results (SI section 3 for test procedure, Supplementary Movie 7). 2.4. Curvature sensor
Curvature sensors are a type of proprioceptive sensor that combines pressure data and bending data. These sensors serve two main purposes: (1) providing bending state information that complement tactile measurements, and (2) enabling load estimation and slip detection. However, the primary function is to monitor the bending state of each finger during grasping. This feedback is essential because it is an underactuated system where all fingers are actuated simultaneously. Curvature sensing allows us to confirm that each finger bends sufficiently to establish stable contact and apply the required force without damaging the fruit.

In Fig. 5a, we present a fully integrated optical fiber sensor embedded in a gripper’s finger, along with an image illustrating red light traveling through the optical fiber from the transmission end (red LED) to the receiver (phototransistor). We designed the finger actuator to function as a curvature sensor. We created a U-shaped channel measuring 0.8 mm in diameter on the palmar side of the finger cover and installed 23 soft clamps to secure the fiber along this channel. The sensor design and characterization procedures are described in EM section 4.7 and SI section 6.

In Fig. 5b, we report the total light received at the phototransistor's end, expressed as voltage output over time at various bending angles. Fig. 5c displays a superimposed image of the gripper with the integrated light guide, highlighting its corresponding bending angles at different applied pressures. We converted the voltage output data into light intensity loss (dB) using Beer-Lambert’s Law, as represented by the following equation22:
Light Intensity Loss (dB) = 10×log 10 (V0/V)

The curvature sensor results indicate that light intensity initially increased from 3.58 dB to 5.09 dB as the bending angle increased from 0° to 77.47°. The bending, however, continued from 77.47° to 211°, and the light intensity dropped to -7 dB, suggesting a critical bending angle for sensor measurements. Fig. 5d plots bending angles against their corresponding light intensity variations at different input pressures. The initial increase in light loss can be explained by our sensor assembly process. While integrating the fibers into the finger, there is micro-bending between the fibers and the clamps, due to minimal compressive loading. This slight bending produces a characteristic response during finger bending at small bends, the stress relaxes, the bends straighten, and the optical signal changes gradually, whereas beyond a critical angle (~75–80°) the fibers enter tensile stretch, and the light intensity decreases sharply. However, the raw data are non-monotonic, which can be compensated by normalizing the light-loss signal with the gripper’s internal pressure (Fig. 5d). This normalization transforms the response into a monotonic relationship that can be directly interpreted as bending angle versus normalized light loss (see Supplementary Fig. 12). Additionally, we demonstrated that the curvature sensor can be used for load capacity estimation and slip detection. We integrated this sensor into the gripper and tested it by holding various loads (200 g, 400 g, and 600 g) at different pressures (70, 80, and 90 kPa). The results showed that the light intensity dropped by 50% when holding 600 g compared to 200 g, effectively capturing load variations. Furthermore, the sensor successfully detected instances of weight slipping, demonstrating its capability to not only sense bending but also detect grasping failures (Fig. 5e). This capability also allowed detection of slipping events during heavy or unstable grasps. While the present study focuses on demonstrating integrated sensing, we envision applying this capability in future automated harvesting systems to sort fruit into weight categories (light, average, heavy).
