## Methods

4.1. Gripper design and fabrication
The dimensions of gripper components are as follows: the finger actuator has bases measuring 21.85 mm and 10 mm, legs of 52.83 mm, and a height of 12 mm. The finger holder has a pentagonal shape, with each side measuring 22.35 mm and a height of 20.75 mm. Each face of the holder features a rectangular cavity measuring 11 mm by 8.95 mm by 5.65 mm, with an inlet tube for attaching the actuators. The holder also includes a slot for a camera and a ToF sensor, along with additional slots for the laser diode and phototransistor mounts (Fig. 1a and Supplementary Fig. 1).

To fabricate the gripper, we used a multi-step process. First, we designed 3D models of the finger actuators, the holder, and other components in SolidWorks 2022 (SolidWorks corps). To simplify printing, each finger actuator was split into two parts: a finger cover and a finger body. In contrast, the finger holder was designed as a single piece. Next, we printed the components on a high-resolution DLS printer (Carbon M1, Carbon Inc.). Finally, we assembled the printed parts using thermal baking (see SI Section 1 for details) and fastening methods such as adhesive bonding, screws, and nuts.

The gripper construction follows a multi-material approach, combining both soft and rigid components. Each finger is made of a soft silicone-polyurethane elastomer (SIL 30, 𝐸 = 1 MPa, 𝛾 = 3.50). The finger holder chassis, tube connectors, camera, ToF sensor, and laser diode 𝐸 =1.7 𝛾 =0.3). Details of the printing protocols are provided in SI section 1 and Supplementary Fig. 2.

4.2. Rotational module design and fabrication
The rotational module relies on gripper rotation about its roll axis. However, this axial rotation also twists the sensor wiring, power supply cables, and pneumatic tubes. To prevent these twists, we divided the rotational module into two parts: a fixed part attached to the gripper end effector and a rotating part that connects the gripper to the control unit. We used planetary gear-based rotational joints to link these parts. We also created a hollow central axis and integrated a concentric slip ring, allowing wires and the pneumatic tube to pass through freely, ensuring a secure connection between the gripper and control unit without twisting.

A high-torque DC gear motor powers the gear transmission, which consists of a spur gear and a pinion. The pinion is fixed to the rotating section, while a floating spur gear connects to the DC motor. We incorporated ball bearings to enable smooth rotation and minimize eccentricity45. We mounted the control unit on the outer perimeter of the rotating part and controlled the DC motor with a double-pole double-throw (DPDT) switch (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Movie 1). We used the same 3D printer to fabricate most of the rotational and fixed sections, along with the gears, connectors, and bolts. We printed these components using rigid polyurethane, the same material used for the finger holder. For assembly, we employed a traditional method using screws and bolts. The detailed printing protocol is discussed in SI section 1.

4.3. Finger bending characterization
We printed a finger actuator with an integrated rigid body to house the laser diode, phototransistor, and pneumatic tube connectors (see Fig. 2d). We then secured the rigid body to a table using a bench vise. To track the bending angle, we placed grid paper behind the actuator and marked the finger with permanent markers. We positioned a tripod-mounted mobile phone camera (with at least 10 megapixels (MP) resolution) at a fixed distance from the finger actuator, ensuring consistent focus and preventing any camera movement during the experiment. We measured the bending angle of the finger actuator at pressure inputs ranging from 0.1 to 1 bar, in increments of 0.1 bar. We used a constant air source with a pressure regulator to maintain a stable air supply. For each pressure setting, we held the pressure for 60 seconds to achieve quasi-static conditions before taking a photograph of the actuator. Afterward, we imported the images into ImageJ, an open-source software, to determine the relationship between bending angle and pressure. We present all results in Section 2.

4.4. Finite element method simulation
We used Ansys 2022 software to conduct finite element simulations and assess the mechanical feasibility of a soft robotic gripper. Our simulations analyzed bending angles, blocking force, and overall gripper response. We examined total displacement (mm), total strain (mm/mm), and equivalent von Mises stress (MPa) for both individual fingers and the entire gripper. To develop the simulation model, we imported SolidWorks files into Ansys Workbench 20.1 and applied the Static Structural module. We added custom material properties to the Ansys material library using elastomer stress-strain data obtained from standard tensile testing (ASTM D412, Die C, 500 mm/min). After fitting the experimental data into a hyperelastic model, we found that the Yeoh 3rd order model provided the best fit, with the following coefficients: C10 = 167,499.9 Pa, C20 = 453.53 Pa, and C30 = 5.5374 Pa. For meshing, we applied a 1 mm nonlinear quadratic mesh, generating 54,514 nodes and 32,908 elements. We set gravity as a body force in all simulations. To simulate the blocking force, we introduced a fixed surface to measure the actuator’s force output. We set contact stiffness for both self-contact and the fixed surface to 200 N/mm³ using the pure penalty method, allowing a penetration of approximately 0.1 µm. We performed nonlinear simulations using the Newton-Raphson method on a 12th Gen Intel(R) Core™ i7-12650H CPU with 64 GB RAM. The bending angle simulation took 17 minutes and 38 seconds, requiring 298 iterations to converge, while the blocking force simulation took 36 minutes and 7 seconds, completing 738 iterations.

4.5. Vision sensor design and fabrication
The vision sensor consists of an RGB camera and a ToF sensor system, built in a collocated configuration. We built a sensor mount that attaches to the center of the palmar side of the finger holder, positioning the sensors side by side in the center of the gripper. These sensors are securely fixed and move with the gripper. For vision, we used a commercial Raspberry Pi camera with a 5-megapixel Arducam 1/4-inch Omnivision OV5647 sensor, featuring a fixed-focus lens, a 160° field of view, and a frame rate of 30 fps, suitable for Raspberry Pi 4 B. For depth sensing, we integrated a ToF Laser Range Finder with a 940 nm laser detector (VL53L0X) capable of measuring distances up to 2 meters. Both sensors were purchased from Amazon.com. To integrate these sensors, we designed a custom slot that holds them securely through a tight fit (see Supplementary Fig. 4). We fixed the entire mount, including the sensors, using through-holes in the finger holder and double-sided tape.

4.6. Vision sensor test
To test the vision sensor, we built a dedicated setup. First, we mounted both the camera and the ToF sensor on the soft gripper to replicate real testing conditions, then attached the gripper to a 3D-printed stand (PLA, Ultimaker 4). We 3D-printed three standard shapes—a cube, a sphere, and a pyramid—and used three different strawberries. To ensure consistent lighting, we used an Amazon studio box with white light (~832 Lux) and a scissor lift stand to adjust the height of the objects for vision measurements. We used Dr. Meter Lx11330B for light measurements. See Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 4 for an overview of the setup.

Color: We used cubes (side length = 5 cm) and attached stickers with six different colors (white, black, red, blue, yellow, and green) to evaluate the camera’s color detection algorithm. Each cube was placed on a scissor lift at a fixed distance of 8 cm from the camera, and measurements were taken (Supplementary Table 1). For color detection, we recorded Hue, Saturation, and Value (HSV) data and plotted them in a histogram with probability mass functions. The Hue range was 0 to 180, while Saturation and Value ranged from 0 to 255. We repeated this procedure for all six colors, and the results are presented in Fig. 4b-e and Supplementary Figs. 5-7.

Size estimation: For the size estimation test, we used the same vision sensor setup as in the color detection test. We tested 12 distinct objects with four different shapes: a triangular pyramid, a sphere, a cube, and a strawberry. The triangular pyramids had three different edge lengths (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm), the spheres had three different diameters (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm), and the cubes had three different side lengths (3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm). The strawberries varied in size. Each object was placed on a scissor lift, and its outer perimeter was estimated using image data and ToF sensor readings at three distances (8 cm, 10 cm, and 12 cm). To estimate the true object size, we required two pieces of information: (1) the camera’s focal length and (2) the object’s perimeter in the image domain. We calibrated the camera under a pinhole model by placing a cube of known size at various distances and then applied the pinhole method with similar triangle techniques to calculate the actual object size:
f = (dk * v) / h
Where is f the focal length, d is the distance of the object along the principal axis, v is the number of vertical pixels on the square target object, h is the true height of the object.

To ensure the accuracy of ToF sensor measurements, we calibrated the sensor by comparing its readings with objects at known distances. We used this data to develop a calibration curve that mapped the ToF sensor measurements to actual distances and then integrated it into the size estimation code. Additionally, we ensured that the camera and ToF sensor were properly aligned so their coordinate frames coincided (i.e., the camera’s principal axis was aligned with the ToF sensor). This alignment guaranteed that the ToF sensor provided the correct distance between the camera and the object for every measurement.

We also applied temporal smoothing to improve size estimation accuracy across multiple frames. We used a receding horizon filter with a window size of 20 frames, pushing each new size estimate into a queue and dropping the oldest estimate. Several consistency checks (e.g., a shape test and a size percentage error test) were performed before adding any data point to the queue. The output size estimate was then calculated as the average of the 20-frame window (Supplementary Table 2).

Shape estimation: For the shape estimation, we kept the same setup as the previous experiments, except that the objects’ sizes were kept at 4cm. We used triangular pyramids, spheres, cubes, and strawberries for the shape estimate. We only measured the 2D geometry for shape detection, so triangular pyramids were classified as triangles, spheres were classified as circles, and cubes were classified as quadrilaterals (Supplementary Table 3). Strawberries were classified as unknown. The results are presented in Fig. 4b-e and Supplementary Figs. 5-7.

4.7. Tactile and curvature sensor design and fabrication
We used a 0.7 mm stretchable, clear thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) fiber from Crystal Tec Korea (purchased via Amazon). We connected both ends of the fiber to the laser diode and phototransistor mounts. Each mount is cylindrical, with an outer diameter of 5.5 mm, an inner diameter of 3.1 mm, and a 0.8 mm fiber holder. We placed and glued these mounts into slots on the finger holder. Furthermore, for the light emitter, we employed a 3 mm laser infrared diode (1.5 mW, 850 nm), and for the receiver, we used a phototransistor with a spectral response of 450–1080 nm (purchased from digkey.com). When the finger bends, it deforms the fiber, that changes the light intensity. We measure this light intensity variation as a voltage output.

We designed the tactile sensor as a modular, U-shaped conduit—2 mm thick and 10 mm wide—composed of both soft and rigid materials (Fig. 6a). The base conduit is rigid and houses the diode and phototransistor mounts, as well as the fiber. The second layer (the contact layer) is soft and features a 0.8 mm diameter channel with 19 integrated soft clamps along the conduit. We used the same mount dimensions and light components (laser diode and phototransistor) as in the curvature sensors (Fig. 6a).

To fabricate the tactile sensors, we first 3D-printed a rigid polyurethane structure (RPU70) measuring 1.25 mm in thickness, followed by a 0.75 mm silicone urethane layer (SIL30) containing the channel and clamps. We joined these layers using wet resin and then baked them in an oven (see SI section 1 for printing procedure details). Next, we threaded the TPU fiber through the conduit channel, installed the fibers, laser diode, and phototransistor, and finally mounted the completed sensor onto the fingers. We used Black Panther™ 85 (𝐸 = 4.83 MPa, 𝛾 = 1.21) as a detachable adhesive to attach the tactile sensors to the fingertips (Fig. 6b).

The optical fibers for both curvature and tactile sensor are bonded into rigid holders, and the holders are bonded to the fingers, so the relative geometry is fixed during operation. The light source and photodetector (LED and phototransistor) are rigidly mounted to the holder and encapsulated with an opaque silicone sealant, that blocks stray light and further stiffens the source–fiber and fiber–detector interfaces against vibration or shift. Additionally, emitting/detecting elements are enclosed and spectrally separated from typical ambient illumination, the sensor output is largely insensitive to room lighting.

4.8. Tactile sensor characterization
We built and characterized five tactile sensors before integrating them into the gripper. EM section 4.1 provides further details on the design and fabrication of these sensors. We powered each sensor’s laser diode and phototransistor using the same circuit from the curvature sensor tests and recorded the phototransistor’s voltage output through an Arduino Uno. Because the sensor is U-shaped, it offers two contact faces (top and side), so we tested both faces independently for each sensor.

We interpret the sensor’s output as a voltage change, which corresponds to deformation and light intensity loss. However, effective tactile feedback requires both force and displacement information, so we also correlated the force output with the voltage change at a given displacement. To perform this task, we used a micro universal testing machine (maximum 10 N load cell; Cell Scale) to apply a compressive load on the sensor while measuring force, displacement, and voltage. We attached each sensor to the machine's moving shaft with a custom 3D-printed fixture that allows both orientations of the sensor to be tested. We ensured that each sensor face and the object remained perfectly parallel (see Supplementary Fig. 13a-b for the setup).

We tested the sensors against four types of materials: an extra soft material (Ecoflex 10, Shore 00-10, E = 55.2 kPa at =1.0), a soft material (Dragon Skin 10, Shore 10A, 𝐸 = 152 kPa, 𝛾 = 1.0), a rigid material (RPU 70, Shore 80D, 𝐸 = 1.7 GPa, 𝛾 = 0.3), and actual strawberries. We molded the extra soft and soft materials into semispherical shapes and 3D-printed a rigid semispherical shape in PLA (Ultimaker). For each sensor face, we zeroed the load cell, positioned the sensor to barely touch the object, and applied a 0.7 mm displacement under displacement control. We ran seven compression tests per material, sampling force, displacement, and voltage data at 10 Hz. We also captured images at 1 Hz using the testing machine’s integrated camera. We repeated these tests for both faces of all five sensors and presented the results in section 2 and Fig. 6e-g, Supplementary Fig. 13c-d, Supplementary Figs. 14-18.

4.9. Control unit design and fabrication
We designed the gripper’s control unit around a Raspberry Pi to manage inputs from 13 sensors and two solenoid valves. The 13 sensors include one camera, five analog tactile sensors, five analog curvature sensors, one analog pressure sensor, and one digital ToF sensor that communicates via the I²C protocol. We used two digital outputs to control the valves, which brought the total I/O signals to over 70 wires. To handle these connections efficiently, we developed a custom printed circuit board (PCB) that interfaces the gripper’s I/O signals with the Raspberry Pi.

Because the Raspberry Pi only supports digital communication protocols (I²C, SPI, and UART), we used three high-resolution 16-bit analog-to-digital converters (Adafruit ADS1115) to read the 11 analog sensors and transmit their data to the Raspberry Pi via I²C. We also added an I²C port on the PCB for the ToF sensor. To drive the valves, we used two Raspberry Pi GPIO pins connected to a motor driver (1.2 A, 12 V Pololu 8833), which we integrated into the PCB alongside the two solenoid valves. Finally, we linked the PCB to the Raspberry Pi with jumper wires.

The valves require more current than the Raspberry Pi can supply, so we powered them from an external source (bench power supply). We also used an external uninterruptible power supply (UPS, 5 V output, 1A max) for the Raspberry Pi. We routed power from both the UPS and the external supply through a slip ring before delivering it to the Pi and solenoid valves. To accommodate this, we modified a USB-C cable for the Raspberry Pi connection. Supplementary Figs. 19-23 present the complete diagram and circuit design.

4.10. Robot arm control code
For the robot arm, we used the M320 Cobot robot. We took advantage of its built-in drag-and-teach functionality to write a Python script that allowed us to plan the robot’s trajectory. The drag-and-teach feature lets you program a path by physically moving the robot through a series of waypoints. After starting this script in the command prompt, we moved the robot through the desired set of waypoints using manual control by human operators, which were recorded and saved in a JSON file. Once the waypoints were created, we wrote another script to iterate through them, directing the robot to move to each waypoint, pause for a set period, and then continue to the next waypoint. This script would loop indefinitely unless it was halted, ensuring the robot would continuously execute this path (see Supplementary Fig. 23).

Using these scripts, we programmed the four-step path that the robot would follow during the integrated test (not picking fruits directly on the plant). Each test began with the robot in its default position, with the arm extended straight up (State A). From there, the robot moved to a position where the gripper’s camera faced directly downward over the object (State B). Next, the robot moved straight down so the gripper contacted the object (State C). Finally, the robot moved to an intermediate position away from the object (State D). The robot repeated this sequence from State A through State D for each test (see Table 1: Algorithm 1).

Gripper Control Code: The onboard Raspberry Pi was responsible for collecting all the vision and tactile data from the gripper. We developed a single Python script that handled all data collection. The script consists of two main parts: the vision code and the grasping code.

Vision Code: The vision code was the first part of the Python script, running whenever the script was called. It activated the camera and used a computer vision algorithm (OpenCV) to detect objects within the camera’s field of view (FOV). See Supplementary Tables 1-3: Algorithms 2-4 for a detailed description of the algorithm. The script saved an RGB image of the detected object with a bounding box around it, separate HSV histogram files in image format, and a segmented image of the object printed with shape and size information.

Grasping Code: The gripper control code was the second part of the Python script, running immediately after the vision code finished. It collected data from five curvatures and five tactile sensors (as voltage outputs), as well as the gripper’s pressure and the time elapsed. Once activated, it triggered the solenoids to allow air from the air compressor into the gripper. As the gripper inflated, the onboard pressure sensor monitored the pressure. When the gripper reached the desired pressure, the solenoids were closed, maintaining the pressure without releasing air.

4.11. Integrated robot arm and gripper test
For running the integrated tests, we ensure consistent room lighting conditions (~421 lux) for all the testing operations. The integrated test required two separate codes (the gripper control code and the robot arm control code), described in EM section 4.10. We built these codes separately on different devices. The gripper control code ran on the onboard Raspberry Pi, while the robot arm control code ran on a separate computer with a Linux operating system. In the experiment, we ran these codes sequentially, starting with the robot arm control code and then running the gripper control code.

The integrated test includes full-scale robot arm manipulation and real-time measurements of various objects. The robot manipulation task consists of moving the robot close to the object, taking vision measurements of the object, grasping the object with the soft gripper, obtaining tactile and curvature measurements, and then lifting the object and moving it to a different location. We selected various objects to demonstrate the gripper’s manipulation capabilities. Initially, we used synthetic objects such as 3D-printed rigid and soft (casted) hemisphere objects. After confirming the gripper’s performance with synthetic objects, we tested the gripper on strawberries and avocados (purchased from the supermarket). Finally, we tested real fruit picking on a strawberry plant grown in a greenhouse using the gripper’s rotational module.

For the integrated test, we mounted the robot arm on a workbench using clamps. We placed the objects on a separate table next to the workbench with a brown-colored background to create a sharp contrast between the objects and the background. We placed the object on a scissor lift so we could adjust its height and ensure it remained within the robot arm’s workspace. We used an air compressor to supply air to the gripper and a bench power supply to power the solenoids. Additionally, we used an uninterruptible power supply to power the Raspberry Pi. See Supplementary Fig. 22 for an image of the setup.

For the real plant setup, we used a similar arrangement, except the fruits were hanging on the plant, and we programmed a custom path so the gripper would move to the plant and grasp the fruit. See Supplementary Fig. 28 for an image of this setup.

Line 265 As a reader who knows a little bit about optical fibers, I started to doubt the
experimental results presented in the paper. There are coated optofibers, there is a stray
light; and the light intensity variation must be revised. The increase and drop of the light
intensity could be due to misalignment at the source of the light and the photoresistor.
Author Response: Thank you for this comment. We incorporate several design features to mitigate
ambient-light effects and prevent source–detector misalignment. The optical fibers are bonded into
rigid holders, and the holders are bonded to the fingers, so the relative geometry is fixed during
operation. The light source and photodetector (LED and phototransistor) are rigidly mounted to
the holder and encapsulated with an opaque silicone sealant, which blocks stray light and further
stiffens the source–fiber and fiber–detector interfaces against vibration or shift.
We use IR LEDs with matched detectors, and the fibers guide this light by total internal reflection
(but with a critical angle lower than in plastic or glass due to fewer material options). Because the
emitting/detecting elements are enclosed and spectrally separated from typical ambient
illumination, the sensor output is largely insensitive to room lighting. This is illustrated in Fig. 2,
where signals recorded under bright and dark conditions are nearly identical.
Regarding the initial increase and drop of light intensity, this is due to how the optical fibers were
assembled. During assembly, a small amount of IPA was used to seat the fibers in the tight-fitting
channels; after bonding the leads to the LED and phototransistor, the fibers remained under slight
pretension. This produces a characteristic response: at small bends, the pretension relaxes and the
optical signal increases gradually, whereas beyond a critical angle (~75–80°) the fibers enter tensile
stretch, and the light-intensity change increases sharply (see Fig. 5b–d). This behavior was
reproducible across seven independently fabricated fingers in our bending characterization, so we
are confident it is not the result of stray light entering the fibers.
For completeness, we have added the measured ambient illuminance (lux) at the testbench to the
methods and relevant figure captions, and we clarify the mounting/encapsulation details in the
revised manuscript.

In Line 236, which value did author mean: ”the saturation and value...” ? The intensity
would depend a lot on the ambient light.
Author Response: Thank you for the response. We have clarified this sentence in the revised
manuscript and added a further explanation below.
The saturation and value measurements were inconclusive because of the constant lighting
conditions that were used. In color measurements under constant illumination, the hue component
generally exhibits greater variability than saturation or value due to its mathematical dependence
on the relative ratios of the RGB channels. Different colors will cause very different hue values.
In contrast, saturation is defined by the relative difference between the maximum and minimum
channel intensities and value is defined as the maximum channel intensity. Under constant lighting,
these two metrics will remain stable, making them less useful for differentiating object colors
compared to the hue channel.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors present a soft pneumatic gripper with integrated proprioceptive and tactile
sensing. By combining these capabilities with vision, the gripper can assess fruit ripeness and
perform grasping/picking tasks without causing damage. Thorough characterization of the
gripper has been conducted and its potential application in fruit picking has been
demonstrated.
Overall, the paper is well-written and organized. However, the following issues need to be
addressed before it can be considered for publication in Nature Communications:
Authors Response: We thank the reviewer for the thorough feedback and appreciate the
opportunity to address the points raised. Here are our responses to the specific questions raised by
the reviewer.
1. The comparison with related work is insufficient. The authors claim that the proposed
method (collocated camera and ToF sensor + tactile sensing + proprioception) is better
than traditional methods (camera + tactile sensing), e.g., for handling occlusions, but
the strawberry picking demonstration does not substantiate this advantage over
existing techniques. A more detailed comparative analysis, backed by stronger
experimental evidence, is required to highlight the method’s novelty and justify its
claims.
Author Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s feedback. To contextualize our
contributions, we conducted a detailed literature review and added a comparison plot (Fig.
1) that contrasts prior soft grippers and our system in terms of the number of embedded
sensors, the sensing modalities integrated, and the resulting capabilities.
Regarding the benefits of our approach relative to existing methods: many current systems
pair a monocular camera with a single tactile sensor. A monocular camera provides color
and shape but not absolute size without additional hardware or assumptions; obtaining
reliable size typically requires a depth camera or LiDAR, which are bulkier and most often
mounted on mobile platforms rather than collocated on the gripper. In contrast, our vision
module matches the gripper’s form factor and is collocated at the end effector, enabling
concurrent measurement of color, shape, and size. Quantifying contact when both bodies
are soft or compliant is also challenging. We address this by distributing multiple tactile
sensors across the fingers and coupling their outputs with proprioceptive curvature
sensing, so the controller knows each finger’s bending state together with the
corresponding tactile response (Fig. 6 and Supplementary Data). Taken together, these
choices provide the set of modalities needed to capture object features as they exist in
biological systems, which have not yet been fully integrated into soft grippers at this scale.
Concerning occlusion, we performed both benchtop and in situ experiments with the
collocated vision module while the fully functional gripper operated. We characterized
color, size, and shape and observed a shape classification accuracy of 100%, a size
estimation error below 1.8%, and correct identification of six distinct colors, beside
without any intelligent vision algorithm (Fig. 1). Prior work on collocated vision in rigid
grippers has reported improved occlusion handling due to higher visual dexterity, which
aligns with our design rationale and observations [1]
Real-time tests during grasping and harvesting yielded consistent results. While this paper
concentrates on developing a fully sensing soft gripper and demonstrating semi-
autonomous, human-triggered picking, our next step is a fully autonomous control
strategy that fuses vision- and tactile-derived ripeness estimates.

2. The light intensity loss curve in Fig. 5d is non-monotonous, which creates ambiguity, as a
single intensity value could correspond to two different bending angles. The authors should
discuss how they resolve this ambiguity in practice. Furthermore, during grasping, the
curvature sensor may come into contact with the fruit. It is unclear how this unmodeled

Author’s Response: We understand the reviewer’s concern. The raw optical loss–versus–
angle data exhibit a small non-monotonic loop caused by the transition from pre-tension
release to tensile stretch (see Fig. 5d). Because bending angle is coupled to internal
pressure, the optical signal includes pressure-dependent gain. Normalizing by internal
pressure (or, equivalently, subtracting the per-pressure baseline) removes this gain and
yields a monotonic mapping with angle (Fig. 2). For calibration and control, we therefore
(i) operate at fixed internal pressure or (ii) use the normalized signal, which is monotonic
in angle.

3. Given the fingertip sensor’s relatively large contact area, different regions of the sensor
will contact the fruit during picking. How would the tactile sensor’s output (as shown in
Fig. 6f) be affected by variations in the object’s shape, size, and the specific location of
contact? And how would the sensor respond to unexpected shear forces, such as those from
external disturbances during or after a picking motion?
Author Response: Thank you for this question. The fingertip contact areas are
approximately 1.68 cm² (top) and 1.55 cm² (side), while the average surface area of a
strawberry is about 14 cm². Thus, each fingertip covers only a relatively small portion of
the fruit surface, and variation across fingers is minimal. The fingertip sensor measures
optical loss generated by local normal compression of the soft pad and embedded fiber;
the readout therefore represents a spatially averaged normal load over the contact patch.
Object shape/size and contact location can change the patch geometry and moment arm.
We mitigate this in two ways: (i) we regulate the internal pressure to a fixed setpoint to
stabilize normal force, and (ii) we pair the tactile signal with proprioceptive curvature,
so the finger’s bending state is known. In practice, we begin each trial with a small
approach gap and align the fingertip to contact approximately normal to the surface; under
these conditions, conditioning the tactile signal on the measured curvature yields
consistent responses across different contact regions and fruit radii (see Fig. 6f and
Supplementary Fig. S24-26).
With respect to shear or external disturbances, the present sensor is most sensitive to
normal load, but shear produces a characteristic transient: a rapid change in optical loss
accompanied by a curvature change as the contact centroid shifts. During semi-autonomous
tests, the measurement phase was performed with normal approach, and we did not observe
slip; during picking, once all five fingertips established normal contact, fruit removal
proceeded without slipping. In future work, we will use simple rate- and slope-based
features to flag these shear/disturbance events and trigger either a brief pressure increases
to re-establish contact or a commanded re-grasp.
4. The optical fiber for tactile sensing is continuous across the top and side pads, yet these
regions are characterized independently (Fig. 6f). Please clarify how the sensor responds
when forces are applied to both the top and side simultaneously.
Author Response: We have not experimentally tested simultaneous top-and-side loading;
all tests in Fig. 6f were performed with normal contact on a single face (top or side) at a
fixed internal pressure. The fingertip uses a single continuous U-shaped fiber spanning
both pads, and the output is the total optical loss integrated along this path. Based on the
micro-bending/localized-deformation mechanism, losses from multiple contact regions are
expected to add approximately linearly, so combined loading should be scaled with the
amount of fiber that is deformed rather than the exact contact location. In our control policy,
the gripper is ensured to establish normal contact on either pad face, making simultaneous
loading of both faces unlikely during the measurement phase.
5. Fig. 6d reveals a noticeable hysteresis in the sensor’s response during loading and
unloading cycles. This could significantly affect the accuracy of the proposed model.
Please provide a more detailed analysis of this behavior and its implications.
Author Response: Thank you for raising this point. In Fig. 6d, we report the force–
displacement response for Sensor 1 under indentation with a rigid probe; as expected for a
soft viscoelastic pad, this mechanical curve exhibits a hysteresis loop. However, when we
plot the optical readout against either applied force or displacement, the curves for both the
top and side contacts are essentially single-valued with no observable hysteresis (Fig.
S12c–d). The same behavior holds for Sensors S2–S5 (Fig. S13c–d, g–h; S14c–d, g–h;
S15c–d, g–h). These results indicate that hysteresis in the mechanical substrate does not
measurably degrade the accuracy of the optical tactile readout in our operating regime.
Because the present paper focuses on system integration and semi-autonomous
demonstrations, a detailed constitutive model of viscoelastic and rate-dependent effects is
beyond scope of this work.
6. What’s the purpose of measuring perimeters of objects (e.g., in Fig.. 4d)? Just for

Author’s Response: Thank you for the question. In Fig. 4d we report object perimeter as
a 2D size metric derived from the edge map. Its purpose in this paper is to quantify the
accuracy of our vision-based size estimation: it provides a consistent scalar for statistical
analysis and error metrics across objects of different shapes and colors. At present, these

7. Please provide clear definitions for the “workspace area” in Fig. 2e and the “blocking
force” in Fig. 3a.
Author’s Response: For clarity, we define our terms as follows. Workspace area is the
planar reach envelope of the gripper. For each internal pressure, we recorded the distal
fingertip positions and approximated the boundary by a circle passing through the
outermost tip locations; the area is then A=πr2. The maximum workspace corresponds to
the flat state and the minimum to the fully folded state. Blocking force is the normal force
the fingertip exerts on a rigid surface at a given internal pressure; we measured it by
pressing the fingertip against a calibrated scale and recording the steady-state reading.
These definitions have been added to the revised manuscript for clarity.
